name: Build and change the LIS and interfaces
summary: LIS analysts turn approved requests into configuration in the laboratory information system and its interfaces: new client and physician codes and report routing, new or changed tests, reference ranges and rules, report formats, and EMR, hospital and provincial repository mappings. Simple set-ups are done directly in production with a peer check; other changes are specified, built in a test environment, mapped to interfaces, tested with partners, validated by quality assurance, approved by a weekly change advisory board and released in a maintenance window. Changes wait longest in the analyst backlog, for partners' test windows and for weekly approval and release cycles, and failed validation sends about a fifth of normal changes back to the build.

baseline.org_archetype: A large Canadian laboratory company running a central LIS with middleware, an HL7 interface engine, provider and patient portals, and interfaces to hospital systems, EMRs and OLIS.
baseline.notes: One case is one LIS change request ticket, from logging to closure. Incidents and break-fix work go through the IT service desk process.

trigger: An approved request reaches the LIS queue: a new client account, a service desk change request, a clinical trial study build or a new test build with its validation report.
end_state: The change is live in production and verified, documentation and validation evidence are filed and the ticket is closed.

volume.seasonality: Peaks in September to November and before January fee schedule or test menu changes.

evidence.note: Taken from the organisation file process map (volume estimate).

LIS analysts build tests, rules, dictionaries and client codes (s_cln_2026); FTE is the author's estimate from hands-on time and volume, about 9 of the 25 analysts, the rest on support, upgrades and projects.
Interfaces to hospital LIS, EMRs and eResults (s_dyn_hospital, s_dyn_eresults); FTE is the author's estimate; 2 of the 12 are already claimed by result reporting.
System validation analysts in quality assurance validate LIS, middleware and result-output changes (s_dyn_sysval); FTE is the author's estimate.
Weekly backlog prioritisation and change advisory board approvals; author's estimate.

roles.department: Community laboratory testing (The model laboratory Laboratories)

evidence.note: User acceptance testing by front-line laboratory staff (s_cln_2026); FTE is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Log the change request and route it to the LIS queue
steps.description: A request arrives as a ticket from the service desk, a new client account form from onboarding, a study build request from clinical trials or a build request with a validation report; the ticketing system records it and places it in the LIS team's queue.

evidence.note: Request sources follow the organisation file process map; author's estimate of routing.

steps.name: Triage the request and check completeness
steps.description: An LIS analyst reads the ticket, checks that the required fields are present (codes, ranges, routing, effective date, approver), classifies it as a pre-approved standard change or a normal change, and emails the requester when details are missing.

error.defect_description: A change with interface impact is classed as standard.

next.condition: complete, standard change (client code, physician or routing set-up)
complete, normal change (test build, rule, interface, report format)

evidence.note: Standard and normal change categories follow common ITIL practice; shares and times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Obtain missing details from the requester
steps.description: The analyst waits for the requester's reply, chases once or twice by email or phone, then records the missing codes, ranges or routing details on the ticket and returns it to triage.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Build the standard change in production
steps.description: Following the work instruction, the analyst adds or changes the client or physician code, report routing (eResults, fax, EMR), courier stop link and billing account in the LIS dictionaries directly in production.

error.defect_description: A routing or billing field is keyed wrongly.

evidence.note: Report delivery options configured per client include eResults and EMR batch delivery (s_dyn_eresults); times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Peer check the standard change and close it
steps.description: A second analyst compares the dictionary entries with the request, checks a test order routes and bills correctly, and closes the ticket or sends it back for correction.

control.basis: Company LIS change procedure: a second analyst checks every production dictionary change

evidence.note: Author's estimate of common practice.

steps.name: Prioritise in the weekly change backlog review
steps.description: At the weekly backlog meeting the LIS manager reviews new normal requests with their effort estimate, ranks them against client go-live dates, regulatory changes and test launches, and assigns an analyst.

evidence.note: Governance to manage requests affecting laboratory workflows (s_cln_2026); weekly cadence is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Write the specification
steps.description: When the assigned analyst reaches the ticket in the backlog, they confirm requirements with the requester, list every dictionary, rule, report format, billing code and OLIS or EMR mapping affected, and write the build and test plan.

error.defect_description: An affected interface or report output is missed.

evidence.note: Builds touch tests, panels, rules, ranges, critical values and interfaces (s_cln_2026, s_cln_2012); backlog wait and times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Build the change in the test environment
steps.description: The analyst configures the change in the LIS test environment: test and result codes, specimen requirements, reference ranges, calculations, reflex or autoverification rules in middleware, report formats and billing codes.

error.defect_description: A range, unit or rule condition is configured wrongly.

evidence.note: Build content described in s_cln_2026; times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Build or change the interface mapping
steps.description: An interface analyst maps the new or changed codes, units and comments into the HL7 order and result messages, updates OLIS and EMR code mappings and hospital LIS translation tables, and configures routes in the interface engine.

error.defect_description: A code or unit is mapped wrongly for one partner.

evidence.note: Coding and configuration from a conformance profile (s_caristix); interfaces with Meditech, SCC Soft, QuadraMed and Sunquest hospital systems (s_dyn_hospital). Times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Wait for the EMR vendor, hospital or OLIS test window
steps.description: The partner (an EMR vendor, a hospital laboratory or the provincial repository) has to schedule a tester and open its test environment before messages can be exchanged and checked.

evidence.note: Vendor specifications take 2 to 8 weeks and test environment access 4 to 12 weeks for new interface projects (s_nirmitee, a vendor); changes to existing interfaces are assumed shorter.

steps.name: Test messages end to end with the partner
steps.description: The interface analyst sends test orders and results through the interface engine, compares what the partner system displays with the expected codes, units, flags and comments, and fixes or logs discrepancies.

evidence.note: Client validation in a test system against clinical scenarios (s_caristix); rework share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Unit test the build
steps.description: The analyst places test orders on test patients, enters or loads results and checks that calculations, flags, rules and report layout behave as specified, recording the outcome against the test plan.

evidence.note: System testing of individual builds (s_cln_2026); times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Laboratory user acceptance testing
steps.description: A charge technologist runs the bench workflow on the test build (worklists, result entry, rerun and dilution handling, report preview) and signs off or lists problems.

evidence.note: User acceptance testing by front-line staff (s_cln_2026); times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Run the validation script and record evidence
steps.description: A system validation analyst runs a scripted test of the change and of related functions that could be affected, compares expected and actual results including output to EMRs, eResults and OLIS, captures screenshots as evidence and passes or fails the change.

control.basis: Validation of LIS and interface changes before use (computerized system validation) under ISO 15189 and CAP; accreditation (ISO 15189 Plus, CAP, MANQAP) required for the provincial laboratory licence

next.condition: passes; clinical content needs medical director approval

evidence.note: Quality assurance validates information system changes and outputs to EMRs, eResults and OLIS (s_dyn_sysval); change control and computerized systems validation (s_dyn_licences). Failure share and times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Approve rule or reference content changes
steps.description: For changes to reference intervals, critical limits, interpretive comments or autoverification and reflex rules, the medical director reviews the validation evidence and approves the clinical content.

control.basis: Laboratory director approval of reference intervals, critical values and result verification rules under ISO 15189 and CAP

evidence.note: Author's estimate of share and times.

steps.name: Prepare the change record for the change advisory board
steps.description: The analyst completes the change record with risk and impact, validation evidence, implementation steps, back-out plan, the release window and the message to laboratories and clients.

error.defect_description: The back-out plan is missing a step.

evidence.note: CAB review of requested changes to production systems (s_wiki_cab); times are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Change advisory board approves
steps.description: At the weekly change advisory board the LIS manager, infrastructure and laboratory representatives review the change record, check conflicts with other releases and approve, defer or reject it.

control.basis: ITIL-based change management policy: changes to production systems are approved by a change advisory board, separating builder and approver

evidence.note: CAB under ITIL (s_wiki_cab); heavyweight change approval processes slow delivery (s_dora2019). Weekly cadence and shares are the author's estimate.

steps.name: Migrate the change to production in the release window
steps.description: In the scheduled evening or weekend release window the analyst moves the configuration from test to production, or re-keys it where the LIS has no transport tool, and activates the interface changes.

error.defect_description: A setting is missed when the build is re-keyed in production.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of release windows for a 24-hour laboratory.

steps.name: Verify the change in production
steps.description: The analyst places an order on a production test patient, follows it to the report and the outbound interface message, and watches the interface error queue the next morning.

next.condition: defect found after release: fix or roll back

evidence.note: Go-live with close monitoring (s_caristix); defect share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Close the ticket, update documentation and notify the requester
steps.description: The analyst updates the LIS configuration documentation, links the validation evidence to the change record, closes the ticket and tells the requester and affected laboratories that the change is live.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Incomplete request
exceptions.description: Required codes, ranges or routing are missing and the analyst waits for the requester.

exceptions.name: Partner interface testing
exceptions.description: The change affects an EMR, hospital or OLIS interface and must be tested with the outside partner.

exceptions.name: Validation failure
exceptions.description: The validation script finds a defect and the change returns to the build.

exceptions.name: Medical director content approval
exceptions.description: Reference interval, critical limit or rule content needs medical sign-off.

exceptions.name: Defect after release
exceptions.description: Production verification finds a problem and the change is fixed or rolled back.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from ticket logged to change live
benchmarks.population: Author's estimate for a mixed queue of standard set-ups and normal LIS changes

evidence.note: No published LIS change lead time was found. Standard set-ups (about 60% of tickets) take days, so the median falls among them; normal changes take weeks and new interfaces months (design, build and test phases of several weeks each and partner delays, s_nirmitee). The p50 and p90 are the author's estimate.

benchmarks.unit: share of an implementation project timeline spent on interfacing

pain_points.description: Normal changes wait weeks in the analyst backlog behind client go-lives and test launches, which delays new tests and client set-ups.

evidence.note: The organisation file process map states that backlogs delay new tests and client go-lives; durations are the author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Interface changes depend on outside partners' testers and test environments, which the laboratory cannot schedule.

evidence.note: Partner specifications and test environment access take weeks.

pain_points.description: Weekly approval and release cycles add one to two weeks to every normal change regardless of risk.

evidence.note: Heavyweight change approval is associated with slower delivery.

pain_points.description: Ranges, units and codes are re-keyed from request to build to interface mapping, so a fifth of changes fail validation and loop back.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

sources.title: Manager, System Validations (job posting, Brampton)
sources.supports: Leads the System Validation Analysts in quality assurance, who validate information system changes for new assay methods, products and equipment across the LIS (AS400, Omnitech, national order entry, middleware, LabDirector, MedLab) and result outputs (EMRs, eResults, OLIS); product owner of the electronic QMS for document, occurrence and equipment management; supports external inspections by regulators, accreditation bodies and clients; internal audits and periodic reviews of information systems. Salary CAD 72,000 to 90,000.

sources.title: Licences and quality commitment
sources.supports: Accreditations by laboratory: Accreditation Canada ISO 15189 (Brampton, London, Ottawa, Peterborough), CAP (Brampton, London, Ottawa, Winnipeg, Impact Genetics), SCC ISO 15189 and ISO/IEC 17025 (Laval, Brampton, London, Edmonton), SAMHSA (London, Edmonton), MANQAP (Winnipeg), provincial licences. QMS components include management review, internal corporate quality audits, preventive and corrective action programs, equipment validation, change control and computerized systems validation, document and record control, and external quality assessment for all assays (CAP, QMP-LS, Healthmetrix).

sources.title: eResults
sources.supports: Free online results; batch delivery into practice EMRs requires an EMR that meets the model laboratory conformance standards; web service, HL7 and ACORD interfaces; IT service desk handles conformance questions.

sources.title: Hospital solutions
sources.supports: Bi-directional order and result interfaces with hospital LIS (Meditech, SCC Soft, QuadraMed, Sunquest); more than 2,000 tests and test combinations; nine laboratories; more than 500 hospitals served.

sources.title: 8 stages in an HL7 interface lifecycle
sources.supports: Stages: scoping and gap analysis with sign-off by client, vendor and third parties; coding and configuration (days or weeks); simulation testing; client validation in a test system against clinical scenarios; go-live with close monitoring; monitoring; support; upgrade. Interfacing takes 20 to 40% of an implementation timeline.

sources.title: Planning a Mirth Connect implementation: timeline, team and budget (Y. Daga)
sources.supports: Small projects: design 2-3 weeks, build 6-10, test 3-4, go-live 1-2; testing 25 to 30% of the timeline; HL7 specifications from an EHR or lab vendor take 2-8 weeks and access to a vendor test environment 4-12 weeks.

sources.title: Navigating the risks and benefits of implementing a new laboratory information system (Tsui, Venner)
sources.supports: LIS build covers tests, panels, reflex rules, reportable ranges, reference intervals, critical values and specimen requirements plus instrument and middleware interfaces; system testing of individual builds, interfaces and order-to-report workflows; user acceptance testing by front-line staff; issues documented and fixed before go-live with retesting; governance needed for requests that affect laboratory workflows.

sources.title: Practical considerations for implementing a new lab analyzer (J. Shaw)
sources.supports: Team with bench, senior technical and LIS staff; realistic and ideal go-live dates; notify IT of new tests, reference intervals, cut-offs, critical values and comments; check whether new tests need licensing; choose QC and quality goals; enrol each test in EQA or PT; write procedures; hands-on training; notify clients before go-live; post-go-live review.

sources.title: Change-advisory board
sources.supports: A CAB of IT and business representatives advises on, assesses and prioritises requested changes to production systems under ITIL change control; an emergency CAB decides urgent changes; critics cite Accelerate: external approvals were negatively correlated with lead time, deployment frequency and restore time.

sources.title: The 2019 Accelerate State of DevOps: elite performance, productivity and scaling
sources.supports: Heavyweight change processes do not work; enterprises with more than 5,000 employees performed worse, partly because of heavyweight process and controls and tightly coupled architectures.

assumptions: Request mix is the author's estimate: about 59% pre-approved standard set-ups (client and physician codes, report routing) and 41% normal changes (test builds, rules, report formats, interfaces), once incomplete requests are completed. Because the two groups have very different lead times, the median is sensitive to this split: with a 50/50 mix it would be about 30 days instead of about 10.

Shares of triggers: client onboarding 50%, service desk 42%, clinical trial study builds 5% and new test builds 3%. The organisation file has about 250 new or changed client accounts a month, more than this process's 180 tickets, so not every account change is assumed to need an LIS ticket.

Validation of normal changes is done by the system validation analysts in quality assurance, as the company's job posting describes; the same role validates new assay methods in qa-new-test-validation.
Controls tied to accreditation are marked fixed_by_law because accreditation is a condition of the Ontario laboratory licence; the change advisory board and peer check are company policy.

Hands-on time is about 1 hour for a standard change and 20 to 30 hours for a normal change including validation; the stated FTE (about 17, of which about 3.3 are validation analysts in quality assurance) is roughly a quarter of the LIS and integration team, the rest being support, upgrades, portal development and projects.
Loaded costs come from the organisation file (hourly wage times 1.35).
